reviewNote: Compare content transfer with metadata commit, permissions and conflict handling. Chunk hashes validate content, not access rights; atomic metadata publication does not automatically clean abandoned chunks.
capacityExample: At 1m users, 5 changed files/day and 2 MB/file: 10 TB/day of full-file upload before deduplication, retained versions, replication, downloads and metadata. State a changed-byte ratio before claiming delta savings.

reviewNote: Connect upload storage, asynchronous transcode jobs, publishable manifests and delivery caches. HLS is a protocol option, not a required vendor architecture; define cache/revocation boundaries.
capacityExample: At 10k uploads/day, 600 seconds/video and 8 Mbps source: 6 TB/day of source data. At 100k concurrent viewers and 2 Mbps: 200 Gbps viewer delivery, not origin bandwidth after CDN caching.

reviewNote: Separate event ingestion and offline/incremental popularity updates from latency-critical prefix lookup. Completion indexes are one approach; a blocked-term removal path needs a tighter bound than general index refresh.
capacityExample: At 10m terms and 30 bytes/term: 300 MB of text only. Prefix structures, per-prefix top-k entries, counters, replicas and language normalization add overhead.

reviewNote: Follow accepted work through fan-out queues, providers and callbacks. Do not equate provider acceptance or transport acknowledgement with user receipt; expire stale notifications and bound retries.
capacityExample: At 10m notifications/day and 3 channels: 30m delivery attempts/day before retries, about 347.2/s average and 3472/s at tenfold peak. One 500-byte status row per logical notification for 30 days is 150 GB; per-channel history is additional.

reviewNote: Connect frontier scheduling, per-site politeness, fetching, parsing and deduplication. Robots rules are not authorization. Revalidate destination safety after DNS resolution and redirects; crawling does not bypass access controls.
capacityExample: At 10m pages/day and 100 KB/page: 1 TB/day, 30 TB for 30 days of compressed pages before replicas, URL metadata and duplicate savings; average fetch rate is about 115.7/s.

reviewNote: Follow ingestion WAL, series partitions, query aggregation and alert evaluation. Label cardinality multiplies series. The seed uses uncompressed 16-byte samples; published compression observations are not a quota or a universal storage guarantee.
capacityExample: At 100k targets, 100 series/target and one sample/15 seconds: about 666667 samples/s. At 16 bytes/sample for 15 days: 13.824 TB raw samples before indexes, WAL, replicas and compression.

reviewNote: Compare sequencing/OT/CRDT choices without insisting on one. Merge convergence does not provide durable acknowledgement, authorization, transport or presence semantics by itself; design snapshots and offline compatibility.
capacityExample: At 100k active connections and 1 edit/s at 200 bytes: 20 MB/s incoming edit payload, excluding protocol, WAL, snapshots and recipient fan-out. Connection count is not simultaneously active editing count unless assumed.

reviewNote: Separate approximate spatial candidate lookup from authoritative driver/trip reservation. A spatial index cannot enforce exclusive assignment. Movement, stale locations and expiring reservations cross component boundaries.
capacityExample: At 100k drivers reporting every 3 seconds: about 33333 updates/s and 3.333 MB/s at 100 bytes/update. Seven-day continuous reporting is 2.016 TB raw history, before indexes and replicas.

reviewNote: Seat holds and confirmation need authoritative transitions; cached maps can lag. Distinguish this from generic flash-sale inventory using individual seats, hold expiry and a late payment-success callback race. Evaluate alternatives without claiming exactly-once external payment.
capacityExample: At 10 simultaneous events each with 10k peak seat-map queries/s: 100k aggregate reads/s. Do not multiply one event peak by all events unless simultaneous openings are an explicit assumption; hold attempts and live holds are different quantities.

reviewNote: Compare central atomic counters, sharded budgets and gateway leases. Atomic commands on one Redis instance do not yield exact quotas across regions or after asynchronous failover; explicitly bound overshoot and define partition behavior.
capacityExample: At 1m decisions/s across 100 gateways: 10k decisions/s/gateway if evenly distributed. A hot tenant producing 10% contributes 100k decisions/s and can dominate one key; aggregate throughput does not guarantee balanced partitions.

reviewNote: Keep accepted payment, order state, stock reservation and ledger effects separate. Define idempotency and recovery across component boundaries; neither broker confirmation nor a local transaction alone guarantees an end-to-end exactly-once workflow. Newly authored training seed; model quality and numerical consistency have not been acceptance-tested in this iteration.
capacityExample: At 1m orders/day: about 11.6 creates/s average and 116–347/s at 10–30x peak. One year of 2 KB/order is 730 GB decimal before indexes/replicas. At 5 events/order and 500 B/event, events add 912.5 GB/year; refunds and archived payloads are additional.

reviewNote: A sorted set can implement one ranking index but is not the complete authoritative scoring platform. Define stable tie-breaking, event identity, exact-versus-approximate rank requirements and season cutover before selecting partition strategies. Newly authored training seed; model quality and numerical consistency have not been acceptance-tested in this iteration.
capacityExample: At 100 boards with 100k entries/board and 64 B/entry: 640 MB of base entries, before sorted-set structures, deduplication state and replicas. At 100k peak events/s and 200 B/event, peak ingress is 20 MB/s; daily storage needs a separately stated average rate.

reviewNote: Separate identity from authorization and token transport from storage semantics. Require standard cryptography and explicit revocation/failure contracts; JWT alone does not solve permission freshness, token theft or session revocation. Newly authored training seed; model quality and numerical consistency have not been acceptance-tested in this iteration.
capacityExample: At 1m logins/day, average is about 11.6/s and peak at 20x is about 231/s. At 10m active sessions and 200 B/session, base state is 2 GB decimal before indexes, TTL bookkeeping, replication and audit history. Authorization checks have a separate, much larger peak rate.

reviewNote: This is a training exercise, not a compliance specification. Require an explicit ledger invariant, currency model and external payment contract. An unknown external result cannot safely trigger an unbounded retry or an unconditional funds release. Newly authored training seed; model quality and numerical consistency have not been acceptance-tested in this iteration.
capacityExample: At 1m operations/day and two 500 B entries/operation: 1 GB/day and 2.555 TB over 7x365 days, decimal, before indexes, replicas, audit payloads and backups. Peak at 20x daily average is about 231 operations/s, separate from read traffic.

reviewNote: Visitor identity, event identity and aggregation window are distinct. Approximate distinct counts cannot produce an exact membership list or be naively subtracted for arbitrary window deletion. Numerical error and late-data contracts are candidate choices, not hidden mandatory products. Newly authored training seed; model quality and numerical consistency have not been acceptance-tested in this iteration.
capacityExample: At 100m events/day and 300 B/event: 30 GB/day and 900 GB for 30 days before indexes/replicas; average is about 1157 events/s and peak about 11574/s at 10x. Aggregate/sketch storage depends on the explicitly selected windows and dimensional cardinality.

reviewNote: All scale and service objectives are local training assumptions. Ask the candidate to define authority, failure boundaries and degraded behavior; do not prescribe a vendor or require every optional deep dive. Capacity arithmetic below excludes indexes, replication, compression and operational overhead unless stated.
capacityExample: At 10m source documents x 4 KB = 40 GB decimal source payload. At 1000 updates/s x 4 KB = 4 MB/s update payload before transport overhead. Search index size must be estimated separately, not assumed equal to source size.

reviewNote: All scale and service objectives are local training assumptions. Ask the candidate to define authority, failure boundaries and degraded behavior; do not prescribe a vendor or require every optional deep dive. Capacity arithmetic below excludes indexes, replication, compression and operational overhead unless stated.
capacityExample: At 100k clients and a 100 KB bundle, a full fanout is 10 GB decimal. Polling every 30 s averages about 3333 polls/s; conditional empty responses differ from transferring the full bundle. Fanout timing and regional replicas need separate estimates.

reviewNote: All scale and service objectives are local training assumptions. Ask the candidate to define authority, failure boundaries and degraded behavior; do not prescribe a vendor or require every optional deep dive. Capacity arithmetic below excludes indexes, replication, compression and operational overhead unless stated.
capacityExample: At 1bn logs/day x 1 KB = 1 TB/day decimal; 7 hot days = 7 TB raw, 90 total days = 90 TB raw including hot days. Average ingestion is about 11574 logs/s; 10x peak is about 115741/s. Compression and index expansion need independent measurements.

reviewNote: All scale and service objectives are local training assumptions. Ask the candidate to define authority, failure boundaries and degraded behavior; do not prescribe a vendor or require every optional deep dive. Capacity arithmetic below excludes indexes, replication, compression and operational overhead unless stated.
capacityExample: At 1m workflows/day x 10 steps x 3 history events/step x 500 B/event = 15 GB/day and 1.35 TB over 90 days decimal. This excludes retries, wait events and payload blobs. Active workflow count depends on duration distribution, not daily starts alone.

reviewNote: All scale and service objectives are local training assumptions. Ask the candidate to define authority, failure boundaries and degraded behavior; do not prescribe a vendor or require every optional deep dive. Capacity arithmetic below excludes indexes, replication, compression and operational overhead unless stated.
capacityExample: At 100m records x 2 KB = 200 GB logical payload decimal; three complete replicas require 600 GB before indexes, write logs and compaction headroom. At 100k ops/s and read/write ratio 4:1, 20k writes/s x 2 KB = 40 MB/s incoming write payload before replication.

reviewNote: All scale and service objectives are local training assumptions. Ask the candidate to define authority, failure boundaries and degraded behavior; do not prescribe a vendor or require every optional deep dive. Capacity arithmetic below excludes indexes, replication, compression and operational overhead unless stated.
capacityExample: At 1m concurrent viewers x 3 Mbps = 3 Tbps viewer delivery bandwidth, before protocol overhead. At 10k broadcasters x 3 Mbps = 30 Gbps source ingestion. One hour of one 3 Mbps rendition is 1.35 GB decimal; multiple renditions and replicas add separately.
